days.label: Zhuangzi 1.1 to 1.63
days.key: And sometimes I do not reach, but fall to the ground midway. What then can be the use of going up ninety thousand li in order to start for the south?”
days.s: Laughing at the great bird’s climb, a cicada tells a young dove of its own short hops; Guo Xiang, on chapter 1, reads it as each content in its own nature, the great not prizing itself, the small not envying, both equally at ease.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 1, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 1, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6351652 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 1.64 to 2.69
days.key: But what is it that gives to each the individuality, to all the potentiality, of sound?
days.s: Asked what Heaven’s music is, beyond wind in hollows and human pipes, Tzŭ Ch’i answers with a question; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads Heaven’s music as no separate thing but the hollows and pipes themselves, each sounding of itself, with no one rousing them.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 2, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 5978516 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 2.70 to 2.140
days.key: “How do I know that love of life is not a delusion after all? How do I know but that he who dreads to die is not as a child who has lost the way and cannot find his home?
days.s: Answering Chü Ch’iao on the sage, Chang Wu Tzŭ turns to life and death; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads life and death as one, so that delighting in life alone sets itself against change, and death may be the strayed child’s return home.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 3, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6364018 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 2.141 to 4.13
days.key: Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
days.s: Closing the chapter, Chuang Tzŭ tells of waking from a butterfly dream; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads it as each state suiting its moment, so the present life may be a brief doze’s dream, and grieving at death while alive is an error.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 3, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6364018 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 4.14 to 4.77
days.key: Then the soul will be a negative existence, passively responsive to externals. In such a negative existence, only TAO can abide. And that negative state is the fasting of the heart.”
days.s: Counselling Yen Hui before he goes to the headstrong Prince of Wei, Confucius explains a fast; Guo Xiang, on chapter 4, reads it as setting aside ears, eyes, mind and intent, trusting the breath’s own nature, for in an emptied heart the utmost Way gathers.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 5, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907034 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 4.78 to 5.23
days.key: All men know the use of useful things; but they do not know the use of useless things.”
days.s: Closing the chapter, the eccentric Chieh Yü, passing Confucius’ door, speaks of cinnamon and lacquer trees cut down for use; Guo Xiang, on chapter 4, reads it as the useful spending itself on another’s achievement while the useless keeps its own life whole.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 5, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907034 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 5.24 to 6.9
days.key: What they loved was their mother; not the body which contained her, but that which made the body what it was.
days.s: Asked by Duke Ai about a loathsome man everyone loves, Confucius tells of piglets leaving their dead mother; Guo Xiang, on chapter 5, takes the power behind the body as talent and virtue, whose departure at death broke the piglets’ kinship with her.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 5, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 6, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6353768 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 6.10 to 6.106
days.key: But at midnight a strong man may come and carry away the boat on his back.
days.s: A boat hidden in a creek seems safe, though anything hidden may still be lost; Guo Xiang, on chapter 6, takes the ‘strong man’ as change, carrying heaven and earth on to the new, so the self of before is not the self of now.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 6, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 7, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6011742 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 6.107 to 6.193
days.key: “These men,” replied Confucius, “travel beyond the rule of life. I travel within it.
days.s: Hearing from Tzŭ Kung of friends singing over a corpse, Confucius answers; Guo Xiang, on chapter 6, reads outside and inside as one, the sage roaming outside to enlarge the inside, a roaming the text gives these friends lest readers refuse it in Confucius.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 6, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 8, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6354439 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 6.194 to 7.71
days.key: For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.
days.s: Ending a homily on inaction, the chapter turns to the perfect man; Guo Xiang, on chapter 7, reads the mirror as reflecting things without feeling, answering what comes and stopping when it goes, so all the world may come to it without wearying the spirit.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 7, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 9, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6364291 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 8 to 9
days.key: Then he kept them hungry and thirsty, trotting them and galloping them, and grooming, and trimming, with the misery of the tasselled bridle before and the fear of the knotted whip behind, until more than half of them were dead.
days.s: Poh Loh, famed as a horse-tamer, sets to work; Guo Xiang, on chapter 9, takes good driving as suiting each horse’s strength and speed so its nature stays whole, and says that hearing this as leaving horses unridden strays far from the text’s meaning.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 9, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 11, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6355259 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 10.1 to 11.12
days.key: But good men are scarce and bad men plentiful, so that the good the Sages do to the world is little and the evil great.
days.s: Robber Chê having claimed the Sages’ virtues for thieving, the chapter draws its moral; Guo Xiang, on chapter 10, takes the saying as true yet holds that the Sages cannot be dropped while the world’s cleverness remains, their harm being less than lawlessness without them.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 10, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 12, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907033 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 11.13 to 11.91
days.key: Therefore, for the perfect man who is unavoidably summoned to power over his fellows, there is naught like Inaction.
days.s: After eight refinements the world cherishes in error, the chapter turns to the ruler; Guo Xiang, on chapter 11, reads inaction not as folded hands and silence but as leaving each thing to act of itself, so that nature and life are at rest.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 13, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907032 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 11.92 to 12.31
days.key: “Let all things revert to their original constitution. If they do this, without knowledge, the result will be a simple purity which they will never lose; but knowledge will bring with it a divergence therefrom.
days.s: Pressed again, the Vital Principle tells the Spirit of the Clouds to rest in inaction; Guo Xiang, on chapter 11, reads the return as true only when made without knowing, for things left unknowing to return of themselves never leave their root.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 13, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907032 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 12.32 to 12.115
days.key: When ONE came into existence, there was ONE, but it was formless. When things got that by which they came into existence, it was called their virtue.
days.s: A brief account of the beginning moves from the Nameless toward destiny, form and nature; Guo Xiang, on chapter 12, reads it as things getting life of themselves, since non-being cannot produce them, and virtue as leaving them to that self-getting.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 14, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356578 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 12.116 to 13.17
days.key: But Confucius said, “That fellow pretends to a knowledge of the science of the ante-mundane. He knows something, but not much. His government is of the internal, not of the external.
days.s: Tzŭ Kung tells Confucius of the gardener who scorned machines; Guo Xiang, on chapter 12, reads the pretence as lying in his turning from the present to the past, ashamed of the world’s affairs, whereas one truly of that art governs nothing, inner or outer.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 14, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356578 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 13.18 to 13.85
days.key: Rulers must practise inaction in order to administer the empire. The ruled must practise action in order to subserve the interests of the empire. This is an unchangeable law.
days.s: Having praised inaction, the chapter divides ruler from ruled; Guo Xiang, on chapter 13, reads the ruler’s use of the empire as a doing called inaction because it follows his nature, so that, each following his own, no one above or below acts.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 13, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 15, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356924 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 13.86 to 14.68
days.key: “The sky turns round; the earth stands still; sun and moon pursue one another. Who causes this? Who directs this?
days.s: A new chapter opens with questions about the motions of sky, clouds and wind; Guo Xiang, on chapter 14, reads the sky as moving, the earth as resting and sun and moon as taking turns, each of itself, with no one causing or directing them.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 16, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6365115 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 14.69 to 14.134
days.key: Foot-prints are made by the shoe: they are not the shoe itself.
days.s: Lao Tzŭ tells Confucius, whose Six Canons no ruler adopted, that they are old tracks; Guo Xiang, on chapter 14, reads the shoe as what is so of itself, and the Canons as the print of one who leaves each thing to its true nature.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 16, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6365115 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 14.135 to 17.4
days.key: If the age was unsuitable and their mission at failure, they fell back upon their own resources and waited.
days.s: The chapter says the retired scholars of old hid neither body, words nor wisdom; Guo Xiang, on chapter 16, reads the waiting as a sage’s calm in a busy age: deep-rooted, he waits for things to act of themselves, so the Way is not lost.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 16, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 18, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6365330 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 17.5 to 17.70
days.key: In the universe I am but as a small stone or a small tree on a vast mountain.
days.s: Praised by the humbled River, the Spirit of the Ocean declines to boast; Guo Xiang, on chapter 17, reads the words as seeming to belittle the small beside the great, though their sense is that each thing, knowing its limit, rests in its portion.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 17, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 19, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907030 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 17.71 to 17.152
days.key: Your very question shows that you knew I knew.
days.s: On the Hao bridge, Hui Tzŭ denies anyone but a fish can know its pleasure; Guo Xiang, on chapter 17, reads it as saying no one need be a fish to know fishes, since Hui Tzŭ knew Chuang Tzŭ was no fish without being him.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 17, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 19, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907030 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 18.1 to 19.7
days.key: At this, the skull opened its eyes wide and knitted its brows and said, “How should I cast aside happiness greater than that of a king, and mingle once again in the toils and troubles of mortality?”
days.s: Offered in a dream a return to flesh and kin, the skull Chuang Tzŭ slept on replies; Guo Xiang, on chapter 18, reads it as setting life and death level, at peace in each, and denies an older view that Chuang Tzŭ loved death.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 18, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 20, Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5978526 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 19.8 to 19.92
days.key: “Do not develop your artificial intelligence, but develop that intelligence which is from God. From the latter, results virtue; from the former, cunning.
days.s: Late in Kuan Yin’s answer to Lieh Tzŭ, two kinds of knowing are contrasted; Guo Xiang, on chapter 19, reads the one from God as nature moving without forethought, content with enough, and the artificial as knowledge in use, chasing whatever stirs it endlessly.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 19, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 21, Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907029 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 19.93 to 20.41
days.key: How then can there be any fixed point? Alas indeed! Take note, my disciples, that such is to be found only in the domain of TAO.”
days.s: Pressed by a disciple over the useless tree spared and useless goose killed, Chuang Tzŭ turns to how human affairs reverse; Guo Xiang, on chapter 20, reads it as no one method fitting the uncertain: only one changing with the times gets through every change.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 20, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 22, Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5978310 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 20.42 to 21.11
days.key: That of the superior man passes from the negative to the affectionate. That of the mean man passes from the full-flavoured to nothing.
days.s: Sang Hu, asked why Confucius’ friends have left him, contrasts friendships like water and wine; Guo Xiang, on chapter 20, reads the first as bland without profit and close through the Way, the second as sweet with profit, which never lasts, and so broken off.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 20, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 22, Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5978310 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 21.12 to 21.98
days.key: Nevertheless, why should you grieve? Although my old self is constantly passing away, there remains that which does not pass away.”
days.s: To Yen Yüan, who cannot keep up with him, Confucius says the self he follows is already gone; Guo Xiang, on chapter 21, reads what remains as daily renewal: the old self forgotten, a new self already come, and never other than himself.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 21, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 23, Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907028 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 21.99 to 22.67
days.key: What we love is animation. What we hate is corruption. But corruption in its turn becomes animation, and animation once more becomes corruption.
days.s: Answering Knowledge, the Yellow Emperor treats life and death as one vital fluid gathering and dispersing; Guo Xiang, on chapter 22, reads animation and corruption as what each likes and hates, one’s liking another’s loathing, so death and life, self and other, do not differ.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 22, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 24, Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907027 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 22.68 to 23.2
days.key: Do not therefore insist in any particular direction; for there is nothing which escapes. Such is perfect TAO; and such also is ideal speech.
days.s: Having named the ant, a potsherd and ordure to Tung Kuo Tzŭ as places of TAO, Chuang Tzŭ defends going so low; Guo Xiang, on chapter 22, explains that a TAO absent from anything would not reach everywhere, and so would not be TAO.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 22, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907027 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 23.3 to 23.92
days.key: “The Portal of God is Non-Existence. All things sprang from Non-Existence. Existence could not make existence existence.
days.s: Having defined Space and Time, the passage names the gate through which birth and death pass; Guo Xiang, on chapter 23, reads it as saying that what exists exists of itself, so the portal is no portal, and non-existence does not produce existence.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 23, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6359136 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 23.93 to 24.50
days.key: “Love for the people is the root of all evil to the people. Cultivation of duty towards one’s neighbour in order to put an end to war is the origin of all fighting.
days.s: Asked by the Prince whether love and duty can end war, Hsü Wu Kuei says no; Guo Xiang, on chapter 24, explains that love, once shown and prized, is already false, and duty makes names shine, stirring a rivalry no wish for peace can end.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 24, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907021 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 24.51 to 24.171
days.key: “And I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak.”
days.s: Passing Hui Tzŭ’s grave, Chuang Tzŭ likens himself to a mason whose steady partner has died; Guo Xiang, on chapter 24, reads it as saying that without a partner who stays unmoved and forgets words, even the utmost speech has nowhere to be used.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 24, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907021 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 24.172 to 25.27
days.key: “The love of a Sage for his fellows likewise finds expression among mankind. Were he not told so, he would not know that he loved his fellows.
days.s: After the beauty who knows her beauty only when told, the passage turns to the Sage’s love; Guo Xiang, on chapter 25, explains that the Sage, like a mirror, has no love, but because his work helps things, people give him that name.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 25, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5978511 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 25.28 to 25.126
days.key: In the Wei State there is the city of Liang. In the city of Liang there is a prince. In what does that prince differ from Violence?”
days.s: Tai Chin Jen, answering Prince Hui’s anger at Ch’i, tells of a snail’s warring horns; Guo Xiang, on chapter 25, explains that the prince and Violence are alike bounded, nothing beside the boundless, so a prince within Liang is not worth fighting over.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 25, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5978511 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 25.127 to 26.73
days.key: Get rid of small wisdom, and great wisdom will shine upon you. Put away goodness and you will be naturally good.
days.s: Confucius, drawing the moral of the divine tortoise, speaks of the limits of wisdom; Guo Xiang, on chapter 26, reads small knowing as serving the self and great knowing as leaving things be, and goodness put away as no longer longed for, and so unforced.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 26, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu juan 28, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5978513 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 26.74 to 28.11
days.key: But language which flows constantly over, as from a full goblet, is in accord with God.
days.s: The chapter opens by naming three kinds of speech, of which this is the third; Guo Xiang, on chapter 27, reads the goblet, tipping when full and righting when empty, as speech that follows things, new daily, filling its natural share and so in harmony.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 27, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu juan 29, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907026 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 28.12 to 28.85
days.key: Thus it is that men like Yen Ho hate wealth and power.
days.s: Yen Ho, sought by the prince of Lu, is gone when the messengers return; Guo Xiang, closing chapter 28, reads its refusals as meant to stir a wind of lofty yielding and withdrawal that makes even the greedy at court sigh at times.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 28, closing note, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu juan 30, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5985055 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 28.86 to 29.26
days.key: Thereupon he took a stone on his back and jumped into the river Lu.
days.s: Offered the throne after T’ang’s conquest, Wu Kuang, like Pien Sui before him, kills himself; Guo Xiang, on chapter 28, reads both as dying for name and loftiness, not as holding the empire light, since one who holds nothing weighty has nowhere to die.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 28, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu juan 30, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 5985055 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 29.27 to 29.115
days.key: “The above instances have been handed down to us from antiquity and are discussed in modern times. They show that men of learning emphasized their precepts by carrying them out in practice; and that consequently they paid the penalty and fell into these calamities.”
days.s: Wu Yoh, called to arbitrate, ends his list of the upright brought to grief; Guo Xiang, on chapter 29, reads the section as saying prized conduct turns forced and prized scholars false, so both are slighted to keep the inner whole, and then stand high.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 29, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu juan 31, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6005747 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 29.116 to 30.43
days.key: “Wherefore, if reputation is not to be enjoyed and wealth is not to be secured, how pitiable it is that men should harass their minds and wear out their bodies in such pursuits!”
days.s: Complacency, having counted six curses of the rich man, from confusion to fear, closes his answer to Discontent; Guo Xiang, at the close of the exchange in chapter 29, reads it as saying that one who knows what is enough always has enough.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 29, closing note, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu juan 31, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6005747 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 31.1 to 32.7
days.key: To see a Sage and not to honour him, is not to be in charity with man. Unless you are in charity with man, you cannot humble yourself before a fellow-creature.
days.s: Confucius answers Tzŭ Lu’s protest at his bows to the old fisherman; Guo Xiang, in his one note on chapter 31, reads the chapter as showing one at ease without withdrawing to rivers and seas humbling himself before their recluse, his openness reaching every creature.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 31, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition, juan 33), revision 6011291 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 32.8 to 32.109
days.key: Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is.
days.s: Closing the tale of Huan, who killed himself when his father sided with his Mihist brother, the passage turns to its moral; Guo Xiang, on chapter 32, reads the reward as answering a man’s nature, not his doing, since study only completes that nature.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 32, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition, juan 34), revision 7907025 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 32.110 to 33.42
days.key: He who does not separate from the Source is one with God. He who does not separate from the essence is a spiritual man. He who does not separate from the reality is a perfect man.
days.s: Early in the chapter’s survey of the schools, the passage names the highest kinds of man; Guo Xiang, on chapter 33, reads them, with the true Sage after them, as four names for one man, differing only in the standpoint from which each is spoken.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 33, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition, juan 35), revision 6366211 (2026)

days.label: Zhuangzi 33.43 to 33.143
days.key: Hui Tzŭ was a man of many ideas. His works would fill five carts. But his doctrines are paradoxical, and his terms are used ambiguously.
days.s: The survey of the schools ends with Hui Tzŭ and his paradoxes; Guo Xiang, in his note closing chapter 33, reads the verdict as exposing the hearsay that had passed those paradoxes off as Chuang Tzŭ’s own and counted him a dialectician.
days.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 33, zh.wikisource (the Zhengtong Daozang edition, juan 35), revision 6366211 (2026)
